title: Time-Series & Geospatial
tagline: time as a dimension — ordering events and locating them in space

options: A sequence of data points indexed in time order
placementQuiz.explain: A time-series is a sequence of data points collected at successive time intervals, where time is the primary index.

placementQuiz.q: Which SQL function extracts the year from a timestamp?
placementQuiz.explain: All three work depending on dialect: YEAR() in MySQL, EXTRACT() in PostgreSQL, DATEPART() in SQL Server.

placementQuiz.q: What is a geospatial point represented as in PostGIS?
placementQuiz.explain: PostGIS uses POINT(longitude latitude) - x=longitude, y=latitude, following the OGC standard.

placementQuiz.q: A time-series with regular intervals is called:
placementQuiz.explain: Regular time-series have observations at consistent, predictable intervals (e.g., hourly sensor readings).

placementQuiz.q: Which operation finds the nearest neighbor in geospatial data?
placementQuiz.explain: ST_Distance calculates the distance between geometries, commonly used with ORDER BY and LIMIT for nearest neighbor searches.

sections.title: Mental Model — Time as a Dimension

blocks.md: **Time-series data adds a temporal dimension to your data — every observation has a 'when' alongside its 'what' and 'where'.**

Think of time-series data as a movie rather than a photograph. Each frame has a timestamp, and the sequence reveals patterns — trends, cycles, anomalies — that a single snapshot cannot. Add location, and you get spatio-temporal data: a storm's path, a delivery truck's route, a disease outbreak's spread.

items: Time is ordered — observations have a natural sequence
Intervals can be regular (hourly) or irregular (event-driven)
Spatial data adds geometry: points, lines, polygons

blocks.label: timestamp types
blocks.code:
-- PostgreSQL
TIMESTAMP           -- no timezone, 8 bytes
TIMESTAMPTZ         -- with timezone, 8 bytes
DATE                -- date only, 4 bytes

-- MySQL
DATETIME            -- no timezone, 8 bytes
TIMESTAMP           -- converts to/from UTC, 4 bytes

-- SQL Server
DATETIME2           -- high precision, 6-8 bytes
DATETIMEOFFSET      -- with timezone offset
blocks.pg: -- PostgreSQL: TIMESTAMPTZ is preferred for timezone-aware apps
blocks.py-pandas:
# pandas
pd.Timestamp('2024-01-15 14:30:00')
# timezone aware
pd.Timestamp('2024-01-15 14:30:00', tz='UTC')
# timezone naive
pd.Timestamp('2024-01-15 14:30:00')

from shapely.geometry import Point, LineString, Polygon

blocks.md: Every geometry has an SRID (Spatial Reference System Identifier). SRID 4326 = WGS 84 (GPS lat/lon). SRID 3857 = Web Mercator (web maps). Always set SRID for distance/area calculations to be meaningful.

blocks.label: setting & transforming SRID
blocks.pg:
-- Always use ST_Transform for distance/area
-- 4326 = degrees (not meters!)
blocks.py-pandas:
# pyproj for transformations
from pyproj import Transformer
transformer = Transformer.from_crs('epsg:4326', 'epsg:3857')
x, y = transformer.transform(lon, lat)

items.explain: SRID 4326 = WGS 84 geographic coordinate system (latitude/longitude in degrees).
In geographic CRS (4326), ST_Distance returns degrees. Use ST_Transform to a projected CRS (e.g., 3857) for meters.

blocks.label: trajectory as linestring
blocks.code:
-- Build trajectory from point observations
SELECT vehicle_id,
       ST_MakeLine(geom ORDER BY ts) AS trajectory,
       MIN(ts) AS start_time,
       MAX(ts) AS end_time
FROM gps_points
WHERE vehicle_id = 'V123'
GROUP BY vehicle_id;

-- Segment trajectory by speed
SELECT ST_Segmentize(trajectory, 100) AS segmented
FROM trajectories;
blocks.pg:
-- ST_MakeLine with ORDER BY creates trajectory
-- ST_Length on geography = meters
blocks.mysql: -- MySQL: ST_MakeLine not available; use ST_LineFromText on WKT
blocks.py-pandas:
# Pandas: sort by time, group by ID
points.sort_values('ts').groupby('id')['geometry'].apply(LineString)

blocks.label: find events near a moving object
blocks.code:
-- Find sensors within 1km of vehicle at each timestamp
SELECT s.sensor_id, v.vehicle_id, v.ts
FROM vehicles v
JOIN sensors s
  ON ST_DWithin(
    ST_Transform(v.geom, 3857),
    ST_Transform(s.geom, 3857),
    1000  -- 1km in meters (3857 = meters)
)
WHERE v.ts BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-02';

-- Time-windowed spatial join
SELECT * FROM events e
JOIN sensors s
  ON ST_DWithin(e.geom, s.geom, 500)
 AND e.ts BETWEEN s.active_from AND s.active_to;
blocks.pg:
-- ST_DWithin with transformed geometries for meter-based distance
-- Time window + spatial filter = spatio-temporal join
blocks.py-pandas:
# Spatial join with time filter
merged = gpd.sjoin(points, polygons, how='inner', predicate='within')
merged = merged[(merged['ts'] >= merged['start']) & (merged['ts'] <= merged['end'])]

revisionCard: TIMESTAMPTZ vs TIMESTAMP vs DATE — choose based on timezone needs
date_trunc('unit', ts) truncates to bucket boundary (hour, day, month)
generate_series creates regular time sequences; date_trunc buckets timestamps
PostGIS: POINT(lon lat), LINESTRING, POLYGON — SRID 4326 = WGS84
ST_Distance on geography = meters; on geometry(4326) = degrees
ST_DWithin + ST_Transform(3857) for meter-based radius searches
ST_MakeLine(geom ORDER BY ts) builds trajectories from points
date_trunc + GROUP BY = time bucketing; generate_series = gap filling

glossary.def: Timestamp with timezone — stored as UTC, displayed in session timezone.
Truncates timestamp to specified precision (hour, day, month, etc.).
Generates a series of values (dates, numbers) — useful for gap filling.
Spatial Reference System Identifier — defines coordinate system (4326 = WGS84).
PostGIS type for geodesic calculations on sphere (meters, degrees).
PostGIS type for planar calculations on projected coordinates.
Returns true if geometries are within specified distance (supports geography).
